title: Dizzy's development and Freddy Webster's Stardust
summary: Mingus claims Webster influenced Dizzy and Bird; he heard him with Lunceford with the audience in tears.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Yeah. What about his -- you were talking about Miles. How do you feel about Dizzy's work as it's gone through the years, his playing?
Well, Dizzy himself, after he started playing like Charlie Parker on trumpet --
Yeah.
He (unintelligible) from that. He progresses in what he's doing. Because he loves to play, loves to play trumpet. I guess he loved what Bird did.
Yeah.
But Freddie Russell was the Webster .
Now, that's interesting, tell me that. I used to hear him on some of the -- there was a Sarah Vaughan record, but I've never heard him live. And I've heard several people say what you just said.
Well, Freddy Russell was the one that Dizzy copied. He was doing those things before Bird, according to Webster .
Yeah.
And Miles loved him, Miles, Dizzy, all of them (unintelligible) Freddy. I heard Freddie in person. (Unintelligible) playing Stardust. I'll never forget
it, man. There were people in the audience, crying.
No kidding. What band was this?
Jimmy Lunceford.
What about the --
It was a big sound, another one of those big sounds.
Yeah. And what was he doing that anticipated what was to come? His harmonies were more complicated --
And his phrasing.
Yeah.
His form of phrasing. That's what Bird was doing so (inaudible). Dizzy was playing like Roy Hutchinson before he played like Bird.
Yeah.
